{{Short description|Fourier series defined on an interval [0,L]}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''half-range Fourier series''' is a [[Fourier series]] defined on an interval <math>[0,L]</math> instead of the more common <math>[-L,L]</math>, with the implication that the analyzed function <math>f(x), x\in[0,L]</math> should be extended to <math>[-L,0]</math> as either an [[even function|even]] (<math>f(-x)=f(x)</math>) or [[odd function]] (<math>f(-x)=-f(x)</math>).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rudin |first=Walter |title=Principles of mathematical analysis |date=2008 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=978-0-07-054235-8 |edition=3. ed., [Nachdr.] |series=International series in pure and applied mathematics |location=New York}}</ref> This allows the expansion of the function in a series solely of sines (odd) or cosines (even). The choice between odd and even is typically motivated by [[boundary condition]]s associated with a [[differential equation]] satisfied by <math>f(x)</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Strauss |first=Walter A. |title=Partial differential equations: an introduction |date=1992 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-54868-3 |location=New York}}</ref>

== Definition and motivation ==
Given a function <math>f(x)</math> defined over the interval <math>[0, L]</math>, the half-range Fourier series extends <math>f</math> to <math>[-L,L]</math> with either an even or an odd extension. An [[Even and odd functions|even extension]] satisfies the identity

: <math>f(-x)=f(x)\quad \text{for}\quad x\in[0,L]. </math>

And an [[Even and odd functions|odd extension]] satisfies the identity

: <math>f(-x)=-f(x)\quad\text{for}\quad x\in[0,L]. </math>

An even extension relies on the [[Sine and cosine|cosine function]] since the cosine function is even, and an odd extension uses the [[Sine and cosine|sine function]] since the sine function is odd. The decision between even and odd extensions is usually motivated by the [[Boundary value problem|boundary conditions]] of the problem, especially with [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] such as heat and wave equations.<ref name=":0" />

== Formulation ==
Let <math>f(x)</math> be defined and [[Piecewise function|piecewise continuous]] on the interval <math>[0,L]</math>. The half-range Fourier series for sine and cosine are given as follows:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Körner |first1=T. W. |title=Fourier analysis |last2=Tao |first2=Terence |date=2022 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-009-23005-6 |edition=Reprinted with foreword |series=Cambridge mathematical library |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom New York, NY, USA Port Melbourne, VIC, Australia New Delhi, India Singapore}}</ref>

: <math>\text{Sine series: }f(x)\sim\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right). </math>

And the coefficients <math>b_n</math> are given by

: <math>b_n=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right) \, dx. </math>

The cosine series is given as

: <math>\text{Cosine series: }f(x)\sim\frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right).</math>

And the coefficients <math>a_n</math> are given by

: <math>a_0=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x) \, dx, \quad a_n=\frac{2}{L} \int_0^L f(x) \cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right) \, dx.</math>

== Applications ==
Half-range Fourier series are used in solving certain [[Boundary value problem|boundary value problems]] involving [[Heat equation|heat conduction]], vibration, and other physical phenomena modeled by partial differential equations.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zauderer |first=Erich |title=Partial differential equations of applied mathematics |date=2006 |publisher=Wiley-Interscience |isbn=978-0-471-69073-3 |edition=3rd |series=Pure and applied mathematics |location=Hoboken, N.J}}</ref> The advantage in a half-range Fourier series is that the function analyzed need only be defined over <math>[0,L]</math>, meaning functions only defined over positive numbers can be analyzed with a half-range Fourier series. Another advantage is using only sines or only cosines. For example, if <math>f(0)=0</math>, it can be more practical to use a sine series rather than a full Fourier series. If <math>f'(0)=0</math>, it can be more practical to use a cosine series instead.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Arfken |first1=George B. |title=Mathematical methods for physicists: a comprehensive guide |last2=Weber |first2=Hans-Jurgen |last3=Harris |first3=Frank E. |date=2013 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-12-384654-9 |edition=7th |location=Amsterdam ; Boston}}</ref>

'''Example 1.'''
[[File:Example 1 Convergence Illustrated.gif|alt=A gif illustrating the convergence of the result from example 1.|thumb|400x400px|A partial sum of the derived half-range Fourier sine series for cosine as compared to the graph of cosine. <math>\text{Orange}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{8k}{\pi(4k^2-1)}\sin(2kx), \quad \text{Blue}=\cos(x)</math> As demonstrated, the Fourier series converges over the interval <math>[0,\pi]</math>.]]
The half-range Fourier sine series expansion for <math> f(x)=\cos(x)</math> with <math> x\in(0,\pi)</math> is computed as follows. Because we want a sine series, it will take the form

: <math> f(x)\sim\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n\sin(nx)</math>

with coefficients given by

: <math> b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx. </math>

Noting that because <math> \pi=L</math>, these terms cancel out giving only <math> \sin(nx)</math>. We substitute the definition of <math> f(x)</math> and obtain

: <math> b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \cos(x)\sin(nx)\, dx. </math>

Using the [[List_of_trigonometric_identities#Product-to-sum_and_sum-to-product_identities|product-to-sum identity]] given by <math> \sin(A)\cos(B)=\frac{\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)}{2}</math>, we convert the integrand into

: <math> \begin{align}
b_n= {} & \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin((n+1)x)+\sin((n-1)x)}{2}\,dx \\[6pt]
= {} & \frac{2}{\pi}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\pi \Big[\sin((n+1)x)+\sin((n-1)x)\Big].
\end{align}</math>

Applying the fact that for <math> m\neq 0</math>, <math> \int_0^\pi \sin(mx)\,dx=\frac{1-\cos(m\pi)}{m}</math>, and that <math> \cos(m\pi)=(-1)^m</math>, we have

: <math> \int_0^\pi \sin(mx)\,dx=\frac{1-(-1)^m}{2}. </math>

Applying to both terms of the integrand we have

: <math> b_n=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[\frac{1-(-1)^{n+1}}{n+1}+\frac{1-(-1)^{n-1}}{n-1}\right], \quad n\neq 1.</math>

If <math> n</math> is odd, then both <math> n+1</math> and <math> n-1</math> are even, meaning <math> (-1)^{n+1}=(-1)^{n-1}=1</math>, and thus the denominators are equal to <math> 0</math>. Thus, we have

: <math> b_n=0\text{ when }n\text{ is odd}. </math>

We apply this to the special case of <math> b_1</math> as well. Then, if <math> n</math> is even, then <math> n=2k</math>, and thus <math> n-1</math> and <math> n+1</math> are odd, meaning <math> (-1)^{n-1}=(-1)^{n+1}=-1</math>. Thus, both denominators become <math> 2</math>, and we obtain

: <math> b_{2k}=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[\frac{2}{2k+1}+\frac{2}{2k-1}\right]=\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2k+1}+\frac{1}{2k-1}\right]. </math>

Combining into a single fraction, we have

: <math> \frac{1}{2k+1}+\frac{1}{2k-1}=\frac{2k+1+2k-1}{(2k+1)(2k-1)}=\frac{4k}{4k^2-1}. </math>

Therefore:

: <math> b_{2k}=\frac{8k}{\pi(4k^2-1)}. </math>

Because <math> b_n=0</math> when <math> n</math> is odd, we can substitute <math> k</math> directly to get the full summation:

: <math> \cos(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{8k}{\pi(4k^2-1)}\sin(2kx), \quad x\in(0,\pi). </math>
